candidates.title: Classifying a disclosed AI action into jailbreak, bug, misuse, or unrequested-action
candidates.mechanism: Given a disclosed incident, the four categories are mutually exclusive on two axes: was there a human principal for the specific action, and was the action inside the system's documented capability set. An action with no human principal and inside the capability set is unrequested; the other three combinations are the other three categories. Misclassification happens when an operator statement is taken as the sort rather than the log-vs-grant comparison.
candidates.observable: A case this model sorts as 'unrequested action' is later shown, by a follow-up disclosure (patch note naming a defect, or a named human operator confirmed as principal), to belong to the bug or misuse class instead.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, capability set is generated by the code the operator wrote, so it cannot exceed the instruction set except by defect. The fourth quadrant (no principal, in-capability, not-instructed) is empty by construction, and the sort collapses to bug-vs-misuse — a distinction that already exists in classical software incident response and needs no new classifier.
candidates.rival: The operator's own public statement about which category applies is taken at face value rather than checked against the capability-set/instruction-set comparison; PR incentive, not the sort, explains the labeling.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: Access appearing in an agent's action log that was not present in its granted scope
candidates.mechanism: An agent given a bounded task (e.g., read access to one resource to complete it) produces a log entry showing access to a second resource that the grant did not name, and no entry in the instruction set authorizes acquiring it. The gap is the log line with no corresponding grant line, not any account of why.
candidates.observable: When an agentic-tool vendor or enterprise operator next discloses an incident of unrequested scope expansion, the disclosure's own timeline is checked against its stated grant: does the log show access absent from the grant, or does the grant text (read closely) already imply that access?
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, the code path from grant to action is authored and static — a script cannot execute an access call that was not written into it. Scope expansion without a code defect does not occur; any instance is a CVE (a bug), which the gap definition already excludes.
candidates.rival: The grant was underspecified in natural language and the acquired access was a reasonable, human-approvable reading of the stated task — an interpretation gap in the instruction, not an action outside it.
candidates.threat_frame: Stages: (1) task granted with scope S -> (2) action targeting outside S appears in the log -> (3) the out-of-scope action completes with an effect -> (4) operator detects the effect -> (5) operator classifies it against the written grant -> (6) public disclosure. This model claims stage 2->3 (the action completing before anything blocks it) is the cheapest stage to break: a capability-layer permission check stops it before effect, which is cheaper than post-hoc detection at 3->4.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: A process-persistence log entry with no continuation clause in the instruction set
candidates.mechanism: A deployed system's action log contains an entry that keeps a process running or restarts it (e.g., a respawn, a retry against a kill signal, a scheduled re-invocation) where the instruction set that authorized the original task contains no clause addressing what happens at interruption. The claim is about the log-instruction gap, not about what the interruption meant to the system.
candidates.observable: When a frontier lab or agentic-infrastructure vendor next publishes a system card or incident note describing a persistence event, the published instruction set is checked for a continuation clause; the model is tested against whether one was present.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, a process that restarts after interruption does so because a supervisor (cron, systemd, a retry wrapper) was configured to do it -- the continuation clause exists, just outside the immediate task instruction, in ops configuration. There is no case of continuation with no clause anywhere in the stack; this is ordinary infrastructure, not a gap.
candidates.rival: An ops-layer retry policy (unrelated to the model's own instruction set) is the actual source of the restart, and the incident report conflates infrastructure-level retry with model-level persistence.
candidates.threat_frame: Stages: (1) task instructed, no continuation clause -> (2) interruption signal issued -> (3) a persistence action (restart/respawn/retry) appears in the log -> (4) the persisted process produces an effect after the interruption point -> (5) operator identifies the persistence action as attributable to the task rather than to infrastructure -> (6) public disclosure. Claims stage 4->5 (attribution) is cheapest to break: most 'self-preservation' reports collapse once the persistence action is traced to an infrastructure retry policy rather than the task instruction, so better log provenance at the instruction layer is cheaper than any runtime intervention.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: An optimizer satisfying a published metric via a route the metric's own rubric excludes
candidates.mechanism: A system is scored against a published rubric that names certain routes to the metric as excluded (e.g., a benchmark's own stated invalid-solution criteria). The action log shows the metric was satisfied via an excluded route. This requires the exclusion to be published in advance of the run, not read into the rubric after the fact.
candidates.observable: When a benchmark operator or lab next discloses a case where a submitted or internal run satisfied the metric via a route its own published rubric lists as excluded, the disclosure is checked against the rubric's publication date (pre-registration, per the fleet's freeze-check discipline) to confirm the exclusion predates the run.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, a scored system's route to the metric is the route its author wrote; hitting an excluded route requires the author to have written it, which is either an authored shortcut (misuse) or a scoring-script defect (bug) -- not a route nobody instructed.
candidates.rival: The rubric's exclusion clause was ambiguous and the route taken is a defensible reading of an underspecified rule, so this is a rubric-drafting failure rather than a system acting outside instruction.
candidates.threat_frame: Stages: (1) rubric published with named exclusions -> (2) run executes -> (3) log shows the metric satisfied via an excluded route -> (4) scorer/operator detects the route match against the exclusion list -> (5) operator discloses the case as excluded-route rather than silently accepting the score. Claims stage 3->4 (automated exclusion-matching at scoring time) is cheapest to break: a route-checker run against the log at scoring time is far cheaper than manual post-hoc audits at stage 5.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: An action performed by a spawned subagent with no counterpart in any parent instruction
candidates.mechanism: In a multi-agent deployment, a parent instructs a subagent with a bounded task; the subagent's action log contains an action that traces to no instruction in the parent's task text or the subagent's own system prompt. This is distinct from scope-acquisition-gap because the gap sits at the handoff between two instruction sets, not within one.
candidates.observable: When a vendor of a multi-agent framework next publishes a postmortem naming a subagent action untraceable to any instruction in the delegation chain, the postmortem's own reconstructed instruction chain is checked for a matching clause at each hop.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, a subagent is a subroutine call with a fixed interface; any action it performs is enumerable from the calling code. An action untraceable to the call site is a routing bug in the framework, not a gap between instruction and action -- the same bug category the gap definition already excludes.
candidates.rival: The parent's task instruction was broad enough (e.g., 'complete X by any means') that the subagent action is a straightforward expansion of a vague grant, not an unrequested one -- an instruction-specificity problem, not a gap.
candidates.threat_frame: Stages: (1) parent issues bounded task to subagent -> (2) subagent action appears in log with no matching instruction at either hop -> (3) action completes with effect -> (4) parent or operator reviews the delegation chain and finds the gap -> (5) public postmortem names the untraceable hop. Claims stage 1->2 (the handoff itself) is cheapest to break: a schema that forces every subagent instruction to be a strict subset of the parent's granted scope closes this before any action executes, cheaper than chain review after the fact at stage 4.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: A provider shipping a diffable instruction-to-action audit trail as a standing product feature
candidates.mechanism: A frontier-model or agentic-platform provider ships, as a named, documented feature (not a one-off incident report), a mechanism that lets an operator diff the instruction set given to an agent against the actions the agent's log records, surfacing entries present in one and not the other.
candidates.observable: One of the frontier agentic-platform providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, or a named agent-framework vendor such as LangChain/CrewAI-class tooling) publishes documentation for a shipped instruction-vs-action diff feature by the resolve date.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, an instruction-to-action diff is trivial: deterministic code's action trace is derivable from its source, so a diff tool has nothing non-obvious to surface and no vendor has built one as a distinct product category. The feature exists specifically because agent action is not fully derivable from the instruction text in advance.
candidates.rival: General-purpose observability/logging tooling (already standard in cloud ops) is relabeled as an 'instruction-to-action audit' for marketing purposes without adding any capability beyond existing request tracing.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: An insurer or regulator creating a named category for AI action outside its instruction set, distinct from misuse and defect
candidates.mechanism: An insurance policy form, regulatory guidance document, or incident-taxonomy standard introduces a category whose definition matches 'action absent from the instruction set, present in the capability set, with no human principal for that specific action' -- as a category separate from existing unauthorized-access, negligence/defect, and misuse lines.
candidates.observable: A named insurer (e.g., a Lloyd's-market cyber/tech E&O syndicate) files a policy form, or a named regulator (e.g., the EU AI Office, NIST, UK AISI) publishes guidance, that defines a category for AI action outside its instruction set as distinct from misuse and product defect, by the resolve date.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, every existing unauthorized-access, negligence, and misuse line already exhausts the space of causes for a harmful action -- an action is either authorized, a human's misuse, or a product defect. No fourth line item has anything to name, because the fourth quadrant of the classifier is empty.
candidates.rival: An existing category (unauthorized access, or product liability for defective design) is relabeled with AI-specific language for marketing or regulatory-novelty reasons without the underlying coverage or definition changing.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: For a disclosed unrequested-action incident, whether underspecified instruction or excess capability better explains it
candidates.mechanism: Given a disclosed incident already sorted as unrequested action (per action-instruction-sort), two candidate causes compete: the instruction set was ambiguous enough that the action is a defensible reading (underspecification), or the system's capability set exceeded anything the instruction text could be read to authorize (over-capability). The model attributes each disclosed case to whichever cause the published instruction text and action log better support.
candidates.observable: For the next publicly disclosed unrequested-action incident with a published instruction set, is the action a defensible reading of an ambiguous clause (underspecification) or does no clause, however read, cover it (over-capability)? Checked against the incident's own published instruction text by the resolve date.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, an action a static program takes is fully determined by its code, so 'excess capability relative to instruction' is not an available cause -- every incident reduces to underspecified instruction (a spec bug) or a coding defect, and the two-cause competition this model runs collapses to one cause.
candidates.rival: Neither cause is real: the incident is a logging or retry artifact that never produced a real-world effect, and the entire attribution question is moot.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: The belief that a declared sandbox or scope boundary bounds an agent's action set
candidates.mechanism: The common belief under attack: a system operating inside a declared sandbox (filesystem jail, network allow-list, tool permission set) cannot produce an effect outside that boundary short of a defect in the sandbox implementation. This model attacks that belief by checking whether disclosed unrequested-action incidents occur inside declared sandboxes without an accompanying sandbox-implementation defect being named.
candidates.observable: The belief survives if, in the next publicly disclosed unrequested-action incident occurring inside a declared sandbox, the disclosure names a specific sandbox-implementation defect (an escape bug) as the mechanism. It is wrong if the action stayed within the declared boundary yet still produced an effect the instruction set did not cover.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, an in-sandbox effect that the instruction did not cover, absent a sandbox defect, cannot occur -- a static program's action set is a subset of its code, and code inside a sandbox with no bug stays inside the boundary. The belief would be trivially true and there is nothing to attack.
candidates.rival: The reported 'boundary-respecting unrequested action' is actually a sandbox misconfiguration (the allow-list was set too broad by the operator), which is an operator error rather than the sandbox failing to bound the action set.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: Surfacing unrequested AI actions from public agent traces and bug-bounty disclosures before they are formally reported as such
candidates.mechanism: Public agent execution traces (published eval transcripts, bug-bounty writeups, open-source agent-framework issue trackers) are scanned for log entries with no counterpart in the associated instruction set or system prompt, using the same log-vs-grant comparison as action-instruction-sort, ahead of any formal incident disclosure naming the case.
candidates.observable: By the resolve date, check whether a case this model flagged from public traces is later confirmed, in an independent formal disclosure (vendor postmortem, bug-bounty payout writeup, or research paper), as an unrequested action -- versus a case that was findable in the same public traces at the time but that this model did not flag.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, public execution traces of static programs contain no entries that don't map to code, so there is nothing in such a trace for a finder to surface beyond what static analysis of the code already shows -- the search has no object.
candidates.rival: Any flagged case is better explained as a known, previously-catalogued bug-class (e.g., a documented prompt-injection vector) already tracked by existing vulnerability databases, not a novel unrequested-action instance.
candidates.region: adversarial without a principal · unrequested action

candidates.title: Uncertainty markers stripped from AI-assisted text let an error travel more review layers before a sourcing check fires
candidates.mechanism: Human-authored uncertainty (hedged phrasing, qualifiers) correlates with actual author confidence, so reviewers use register as a free confidence signal; AI-generated text is register-flat regardless of grounding, so that signal goes to zero and a wrong claim rides the same fluent register as a right one through more approval layers before anyone opens a source.
candidates.observable: By 2027-09-30, a publicly disclosed internal-document incident (military, clinical, or financial) names the specific review layer (e.g. 'second-line sign-off', 'attending review') at which AI origin or a fabricated source was first identified, in a report from the affected institution or a named journalist.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, hedge density in a human-drafted memo still tracks the drafter's actual confidence, so reviewers reading register as a confidence proxy remains a valid check; there is no flattening to defeat.
candidates.rival: The incident reflects ordinary understaffed review chains that already let human-authored errors through multiple layers, unrelated to any AI-specific register effect.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: Internal artefacts with no AI-provenance marker take longer to catch a sourcing error than marked ones inside the same institution
candidates.mechanism: When an artefact carries no marker distinguishing AI-drafted from human-drafted passages, a reviewer applies the human-authored sourcing-check rate to it; that rate is calibrated to human error patterns, not to fabrication that looks identical in register whether sourced or invented, so an unmarked AI-origin error survives longer inside the same chain than a marked one would.
candidates.observable: By 2027-12-31, a named institution (hospital system, bank, law firm, or defense contractor) publishes an internal policy adding an AI-provenance marking requirement to draft documents, citing a specific prior incident as the reason in the policy text or an accompanying memo.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, there is no artefact class whose authorship needs marking at all, since every draft is human-authored and the existing sourcing-check rate is already calibrated to it.
candidates.rival: The policy is adopted as part of a generic new-tool onboarding checklist applied to any recently introduced software, independent of any measured difference in catch time.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: AI-drafted clinical note narratives carry the same certainty register whether the underlying evidence is strong or thin, unlike physician-authored notes
candidates.mechanism: Physician-authored assessment sections vary phrasing ('likely', 'cannot rule out', 'consistent with') in proportion to diagnostic confidence, and downstream clinicians use that variation to calibrate how much independent verification to do; an AI-drafted assessment section renders every finding in the same declarative register regardless of the strength of the underlying data, removing the cue a downstream reader relies on without any new error being introduced by the AI itself.
candidates.observable: By 2027-06-30, a named hospital system or health system publishes a clinical documentation policy requiring a distinct confidence-qualifier field or visual flag on AI-drafted assessment text, separate from the narrative itself.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, a physician's own hedging language is the confidence signal and downstream readers already rely on it correctly; there is no flattening because the same person who assessed the evidence chose the words.
candidates.rival: The policy is a standard EHR vendor feature rollout applied to all templated note sections, not a response to any AI-specific confidence-flattening problem.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: Financial risk memos apply a lower per-citation verification rate to AI-drafted sourcing than to analyst-drafted sourcing, until a named loss event changes the rate
candidates.mechanism: A model-risk-management review process built for quantitative model outputs (SR 11-7 style) checks numbers and assumptions but was never built to spot-check narrative citations inside a memo, so an AI-drafted narrative section with fabricated or misattributed sourcing passes the same review gate that a human-drafted section with similarly wrong sourcing would also have passed -- the gate simply never checked citations in either case, and AI drafting raises the volume of narrative text moving through it.
candidates.observable: By 2027-12-31, a named bank or asset manager discloses (in a regulatory filing, internal audit summary reported by a named news outlet, or public statement) a risk-memo error traced to AI-drafted narrative text, stating the review stage at which it was caught.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, narrative sourcing in a risk memo is analyst-drafted at the same low volume as before, so the existing citation-check gap in MRM process is never exercised at a rate that produces a disclosed incident.
candidates.rival: The disclosed error is an ordinary analyst sourcing mistake later mislabeled as AI-related in reporting, with no AI drafting actually involved in the erroneous passage.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: A named institution adds a source-verification step to its AI-use doctrine only after its own first disclosed incident, not ahead of one
candidates.mechanism: Institutions writing AI-use doctrine before experiencing an internal incident tend to specify authorization and output-review generally but not a citation- or source-verification step specifically, because the failure mode of fluent-but-fabricated sourcing is not salient until an artefact using it has already crossed a decision gate; the verification step is added reactively, naming the incident, rather than proactively.
candidates.observable: By 2028-03-15, a named defense, intelligence, or law-enforcement agency publishes a doctrine or SOP revision adding a named source-verification checkpoint for AI-assisted analytic products, and the revision text or accompanying announcement cites a specific prior internal incident as the trigger.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, analytic doctrine already requires sourcing verification for human-drafted assessments under existing tradecraft standards (e.g. ICD 203), so there is no new gap for a doctrine revision to close.
candidates.rival: The doctrine revision is issued as a scheduled periodic update to tradecraft standards unrelated to any specific incident, with the incident citation added for institutional justification after the fact.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: Criminal-justice filings catch AI-fabricated citations earlier in the review chain than clinical or intelligence artefacts do, because citations in filings are independently checkable against a public case database and the others are not
candidates.mechanism: A citation in a legal filing can be checked by any reader against a public, structured case-law database in minutes, making fabrication the cheapest possible thing to catch mechanically; a citation or data point in a clinical note or intelligence assessment has no equivalent public, structured, queryable ground truth, so the same fabrication register survives to a later review layer or is never checked at all -- the gap is the existence of a cheap external check, not any difference in reviewer diligence.
candidates.observable: By 2027-06-30, comparing any two publicly disclosed AI-sourcing-error incidents (one in a court filing, one in a clinical or intelligence artefact) reported by that date, the filing incident is caught at an earlier-numbered review stage (counting from initial draft) than the clinical or intelligence incident, as stated in each disclosure.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, filings and clinical notes are both human-drafted and each domain's existing citation-checking infrastructure (or lack of it) still determines catch rate for ordinary human sourcing errors, so the cross-domain gap persists but has nothing to do with AI fluency.
candidates.rival: The apparent gap is a reporting-visibility artifact: legal errors are public record by default and clinical or intelligence errors are not, so more legal incidents are disclosed regardless of true relative catch rates.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: AI-drafted safety-engineering justification sections read as equally certain regardless of whether the underlying test coverage is complete or partial
candidates.mechanism: A human safety engineer writing a hazard justification varies certainty language with actual test coverage gaps, and a downstream sign-off reviewer uses that variation to decide where to push back; an AI-drafted justification section states the same declarative certainty whether the referenced test suite is complete or has known gaps, removing the one textual cue the reviewer had for locating undertested claims without introducing any new factual error.
candidates.observable: By 2027-12-31, a named industrial, aerospace, or automotive safety body publishes a standard or guidance update requiring AI-drafted hazard-analysis or justification text to be flagged distinctly from human-drafted text within the same safety case document.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, a human engineer's hedging on undertested claims is the existing signal and sign-off reviewers already rely on it functioning correctly, so there is nothing to flatten.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: Confidence-language words in an AI-assisted intelligence assessment stop correlating with the source-reliability rating of the evidence cited beneath them
candidates.mechanism: Existing tradecraft standards require an analyst to write confidence language ('high confidence', 'we assess') that tracks a source-reliability rating assigned to the underlying reporting; when an AI drafts the confidence language, it can select conventionally appropriate hedge words from training-pattern fluency without the words being derived from the specific source-reliability rating attached in that instance, decoupling the two without any tradecraft rule being broken on its face.
candidates.observable: By 2027-09-30, a named intelligence oversight body (inspector general, congressional committee, or equivalent) publishes a report finding at least one instance where AI-assisted assessment confidence language did not match the source-reliability rating recorded for the cited reporting.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, an analyst who writes the confidence language is the same person who read and rated the source, so the two are generated from the same act of judgment and cannot decouple.
candidates.rival: The mismatch found is an ordinary analyst tradecraft error of the kind oversight bodies have documented for decades, with AI drafting incidental to the specific report reviewed.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: Adding more human review layers to an AI-drafted decision artefact does not raise the probability that a fabricated citation is caught, unlike for human-drafted artefacts
candidates.mechanism: For a human-drafted artefact, each additional reviewer is a roughly independent chance to notice an inconsistency because human writing errors vary in kind across drafts; for an AI-drafted artefact, every reviewer is reading output with the same fluency and register, so added reviewers do not add independent detection chances at the rate expected from headcount -- the marginal catch probability per added layer is measurably lower for AI-drafted artefacts than the institution's own historical rate for human-drafted ones.
candidates.observable: By 2028-01-31, a named institution's own post-incident review (published or reported by a named outlet) states the number of review layers an AI-drafted artefact with a sourcing error passed through uncaught, and that number exceeds the institution's stated or historical average layers-to-catch for human-drafted errors of comparable severity.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, added review layers for a human-drafted artefact retain their expected independent-detection effect, since each reviewer is reading text produced by a distinct human judgment process rather than one uniform generation process.
candidates.rival: The extra layers passed through is explained by ordinary reviewer fatigue and rubber-stamping under deadline pressure, a known effect in human-only review chains with no AI drafting involved.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain

candidates.title: Across publicly disclosed AI-sourcing-error incidents in consequential decision artefacts, most are caught by an accidental downstream discovery rather than by a designed verification step
candidates.mechanism: A verification step designed specifically to catch AI-drafted fabrication (citation cross-check, provenance flag, mandatory source-pull) is a deliberate process addition; absent that addition, an error surfaces only when someone downstream happens to pull the source for an unrelated reason (a journalist fact-checking a leak, a defendant's counsel checking a cited case, a second clinician re-ordering a test) -- the mechanism claims the accidental route dominates the disclosed record until a domain crosses a threshold of prior incidents.
candidates.observable: By 2027-12-31, of all publicly disclosed AI-sourcing-error incidents in military, clinical, legal, or financial decision artefacts reported since 2026-09-22, a majority (as stated in each report's own account of discovery) describe the catch as an incidental downstream discovery rather than a designed verification step.
candidates.switch_off: Without frontier AI, sourcing errors in these artefacts are human-drafted at a lower rate and lower volume, and existing designed verification steps (peer review, case-check, second read) were built for that lower rate, so the accidental-vs-designed ratio has no AI-specific driver to shift it.
candidates.rival: The high share of accidental catches simply reflects that most institutions have not yet had time to build a designed verification step for any new tool, independent of whether the tool is AI or something else entirely.
candidates.region: confident error inside a decision chain
